fr.title: Tu es l’air de ce jardin
fr.description_markdown:
https://youtu.be/3ngWdg8S5JA

Il y a deux semaines, le tableau « Tu es l’air de ce jardin » a été achevé. D’une longueur de trois mètres sur deux mètres de large, cette toile est un jardin composé de lettres : « Tu es l’air de ce jardin ». Tous les poèmes du recueil de poésie « Tu es l’air de ce jardin » y figurent. Parfois, les lettres se sont échappées au milieu des marges. Ce tableau a été envoyé vers notre chère patrie, afin qu’il ait bientôt l’honneur d’accueillir le regard de nos compatriotes lors d’une exposition.

en.title: You Are the Air of This Garden
en.description_markdown:
https://youtu.be/3ngWdg8S5JA

Two weeks ago, the painting "You Are the Air of This Garden" was completed. Measuring three metres in length and two metres in width, this painting is a garden of letters: "You Are the Air of This Garden". All the poems from the poetry collection "You Are the Air of This Garden" appear within it. At times, the letters have fled into the midst of the margins. This painting has been sent to our dear homeland, so that it may soon have the honour of receiving the gaze of our compatriots' eyes at an exhibition.

en.title: Highlights
en.description_markdown: Highlights are the paintings that, in one way or another, have settled most deeply in my heart; I have no other criterion for selecting them: my heart.

en.title: The Chrysolite Vault
en.description_markdown:
A poem by the venerable Hafez guided me to this series of paintings:
Upon this vault of chrysolite it is written in gold
That naught shall endure save the goodness of the generous.
Even though the words of this poem have not been used in any of the works.

en.title: Paintings Whose Colours Have Been Altered with Software
en.description_markdown: I have endeavoured to draw this series of paintings into a different mood and atmosphere by altering their colours through software.

en.title: Daughters of the Nomads
en.description_markdown: Fifteen years ago—recalling my childhood years, when I used to sit beside my elder uncle's shop in the Vakil Bazaar, absorbed in the comings and goings of customers, and saw the shimmering fabrics from my uncle's shop worn by the graceful women and daughters of the nomads of Fars, envisioning them in my imagination as dancing flowers—I asked my mother to send me various colours of these fabrics. The result lies before you: nature, flowers, colour, and calligraphy...

en.title: Beyond Bodies
en.description_markdown:
Beyond the body, unseen lines: through a passage of the body's lines, there are lines that cannot be seen. I have written anew in calligraphy, in the form of painting—my surroundings, three birds within one bird. Seeing, hearing, sensing ourselves and what lies outside ourselves; that "Truth" within us which draws us into play, which awaits us just a few steps away, beyond our reach.

In these paintings, forget the bodies, the lines, the colours, the supports, the names, the concepts, and all that matters to you! Close your eyes and let the first sensation arrive: "Beyond Bodies" is the ensnaring of "Truth"—that point which shines in the darkness of your closed eyes. One day this enclosed space, without exit, will find a way through, thanks to the immense striving of life, and a true light will dazzle us.

en.title: Work with Henna
en.description_markdown: Memories of the use of henna in my mind. We used to draw henna upon the skin to create beauty that would linger on the skin—perhaps so that the skin might also remember something other than the reality of the external world. I too use henna for this very reason. Nature, which is at once beauty and endurance: it is as though one could invent another form of printmaking structure using this exceedingly thin layer of henna on paper, on fabric, or on skin... or upon our own fragile memory...

en.title: I Am Not Myself
en.description_markdown:
[Rumi](https://ganjoor.net/moulavi/) » [Divan-e Shams](https://ganjoor.net/moulavi/shams/) » [Rubaiyat](https://ganjoor.net/moulavi/shams/robaeesh/)

He who has known You, what shall he do with a soul?

What shall he do with children, family, and home?

You drive him mad and bestow both worlds upon him;

He who is mad for You, what shall he do with both worlds?

I, my very I, myself—caught between Subject and object; a singular and profound relationship between them: bewilderment, union, and distance, and at the same time so close that it is as if this "I" were an other. Is this "I" the one I have fashioned in my imagination, or the one that exists in the imagination of the other? Which mirror reflects more truly, or is less distorted? Paintings bearing all these doubts... Hassan Makaremi

en.title: Che Guevara
en.description_markdown:
"Che Guevara" is a song by Namjoo, the Iranian singer and musician. This song is based on the melody of "Hasta Siempre", which was itself written in 1965 by Carlos Puebla. This song transformed me and became the inspiration for a series of paintings. In 2012, when I was invited to Cuba to take part in four conferences and an exhibition, I had the opportunity, through one of the directors of the Cuban Artists' Association, to present one of these paintings to Che Guevara's daughter.

Find him again

Tell him to die again

Perhaps he will take my hand

en.title: Poems in New Harmony and Composition
en.description_markdown: Scattered fragments of forgotten poems do not let me go. They return, settle upon me, and lead me with them to my worktable. It is these very fragments that choose the colours and dance before my eyes—and then depart. I am left with calligraphic letters, like the lingering imprints of the dance of fleeting words. At times, I sense the gentle smile of the venerable Hafez; perhaps he is pleased. Before you lie the footprints of these dancers: scattered fragments of forgotten poems.

en.title: The Plates
en.description_markdown:
And Hafez comes to the plate.

Hours of practice and hours of writing script on paper with the reed pen prepared me for a journey to my ancestors in search of origins: how did they invent a language? How did they invent a script? And then Hafez never leaves me; he has been there ever since I was fourteen years old—fragments of his poems present themselves, remain for as long as they wish, and then suddenly depart.

One day, after hours of practice in the presence of Hafez and my ancestors, I found myself before a plate, and before picking up knife and fork, I saw in the whiteness of the plate the letters dancing and the calligraphy continuing... It is the continuation of my quest, extending beyond the confines of paper.

en.title: Between Signs and Symbols
en.description_markdown: Signs can live alone, separately, without any particular support, without any link between them, across different eras and within diverse cultures; yet symbols and meanings exist together. They are subjects of exchange: every symbol has a past; it is the product of another symbol and, in turn, generates another. Alphabets and the elements of language (musical, mathematical...) form a chained ensemble that expands the environment of our world and our culture, our understanding and our knowledge. The white, the void—that non-sign between signs—is also a chain, a chain extending to infinity. Meaning reaches us from the space between signs. In my dreams, I seek these empty spaces and their meaning.

fr.title: Par l’amour, mène-moi à un tel accomplissement
fr.description_markdown:
Ce tableau en deux volets a été achevé aujourd’hui : peinture à l’huile de 100 sur 150 centimètres. Quant à l’histoire de ce tableau, intitulé « Par l’amour, mène-moi à un tel accomplissement », il s’inspire de la supplique de Majnoun dans la maison de la Kaaba, tirée du poème narratif « Leïla et Majnoun » du vénérable sage Nezâmi.

Il disait, tenant l’anneau entre ses bras : aujourd’hui je suis tel l’anneau à la porte ;
Dans le cercle de l’amour je livre mon âme ; que mon oreille ne soit jamais privée de son anneau.
On dit : sépare-toi de l’amour, car telle est la voie de l’intimité.
Moi, je puise ma subsistance dans l’amour ; si l’amour meurt, je mourrai.
Ma nature a été nourrie par l’amour ; que nul autre destin que l’amour ne soit le mien.
Ce cœur qui serait vide d’amour, que le torrent de la tristesse l’emporte sur-le-champ !
Ô Seigneur, par la divinité de Ta déité, et par la perfection de Ta royauté,
Par l’amour, mène-moi à un tel accomplissement qu’il demeure, même si je ne demeure plus.
De la source de l’amour, accorde-moi la lumière, et n’éloigne point ce khôl de mes yeux.
Bien que je sois ivre du vin de l’amour, rends-moi plus amoureux encore que je ne le suis !
Au cours des quinze dernières années, je viens chaque année en Amérique auprès de ma sœur bien-aimée. Je lui ai apporté de nombreux tableaux. J’avais le sentiment qu’aucun d’eux ne touchait vraiment son cœur. Cette fois, je lui ai demandé de me dire du fond du cœur quel genre de tableau elle désirait. Elle m’a répondu que la calligraphie-peinture l’emportait vers un autre monde. Ensemble, à l’aide du site web, nous avons passé en revue tous les tableaux des vingt dernières années. Nous sommes arrivés au tableau du Simorgh, qui relate la condition des oiseaux en route vers le mont Qâf et ses sept vallées dans « La Conférence des oiseaux » du vénérable Attâr. Dans la sixième vallée, les oiseaux entrent dans la vallée de la Stupéfaction — un volume en forme de tube — et en ressortent de l’autre côté. Du point de vue de la topologie, le tube est un volume qui possède un dedans et deux dehors, que nous pouvons considérer comme le symbole mythologique de l’Iran préislamique : le dedans comme ce monde-ci, le dehors comme l’au-delà, et le dehors-dedans ou dedans-dehors comme le Huitième Continent, parfois accessible, où se dresse le mont Qâf.
À vous de voir comment vous percevrez ce tableau.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/imgserver-1.jpg

Avec un léger travail sur les couleurs à l’aide d’un logiciel, on peut également présenter une image moderne du tableau.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/imgserver-2.jpg

en.title: Through Love, Bring Me to Such a Culmination
en.description_markdown:
This painting in two panels was completed today: oil paint, measuring 100 by 150 centimetres. As for the story of this painting, entitled "Through Love, Bring Me to Such a Culmination", it is inspired by Majnun's supplication inside the house of the Kaaba, from the narrative poem "Layli and Majnun" by the venerable sage Nezami.

Clasping the door-ring in his embrace, he spoke: today I am as the ring upon the door;
In the ring of love I yield my soul; may my ear never be without its ring.
They say: part from love, for this is the path of intimacy.
I draw my sustenance from love; if love should die, I too shall die.
My very nature has been nurtured by love; may naught but love be my destiny.
That heart which is devoid of love—may the torrent of sorrow sweep it away at once!
O Lord, by the divinity of Thy Godhead, and by the perfection of Thy sovereignty,
Through love, bring me to such a culmination that it endures, even though I endure no more.
From the spring of love grant me light, and keep not this kohl far from my eyes.
Though I am intoxicated by the wine of love, make me more ardently in love than I am!
Over the past fifteen years, I come to America every year to visit my beloved sister. I have brought her many paintings. My feeling was that none of them truly settled in her heart. This time, I asked her to speak from the heart and say what kind of painting she wanted. She told me that calligraphy-painting carries her to another world. Together, using the website, we reviewed all the paintings of the past twenty years. We arrived at the Simurgh painting, which recounts the journey of the birds towards Mount Qaf and its seven valleys in "The Conference of the Birds" by the venerable Attar. In the sixth valley, the birds enter the Valley of Astonishment—a tube-like volume—and emerge from its other side. From the standpoint of topology, a tube is a volume that has one inside and two outsides, which we may regard as the mythological symbol of pre-Islamic Iran: the inside as this world, the outside as the other world, and the outside-inside or inside-outside as the Eighth Continent—accessible from time to time—where Mount Qaf is situated.
Now it remains to be seen how you will view this painting.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/imgserver-1.jpg

With a little work on the colours using software, a modern image of the painting can also be presented.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/imgserver-2.jpg

en.title: Love and Oneness
en.description_markdown:
More than fifteen years ago, when I placed the titles of the paintings in this series side by side to prepare the exhibition catalogue, it seemed to me they formed an eloquent poem:
The clouds, as I look upon them, are not so far away,
Like a love without reason,
Like the melody of a hand that sets the other dancing,
They reveal the strange pathways of the universe's genesis,
Like bodies releasing themselves into freedom;
They say to me: behold, we are more beautiful than flowers;
They warm my heart—this voice of the world, this voice of the desert.
Like a hand that sings,
Like my hands clasping you, even when you are not there,
Like clouds that are far yet near, spinning with emptiness around them,
Like time turning, dancing just as they do,
Like my wings flying through the voids of my memories,
Which I seek behind me and find ahead of me—the clouds, I mean—
As I walk towards them and the weight of my body leaves me,
Like inscribing colours upon the carpets that have lived with me,
Like mirrors facing one another, the clouds are not so very far away.

en.title: Nasta'liq Calligraphy and the Compositional Harmony of Chinese Calligraphy
en.description_markdown: The paintings before your eyes are the fruit of my acquaintance with the great Chinese master, painter, calligrapher, and poet Fan Zeng. In 2009, at the invitation of UNESCO in Paris, we both took part in a conference and exhibition marking the celebration of cultural diversity. The title of the lecture, which with questions and answers lasted over three hours, was "A Two-Way Gaze at Calligraphy". Nasta'liq calligraphy, with its smooth and harmonious flow, is the evolution of Naskh and Kufic calligraphy. At the pinnacle of beauty, Nasta'liq calligraphy is the fruit of harmony with the nature surrounding us. Without doubt, this calligraphy is the pearl of the Phoenician family of scripts. This family comprises the largest complex group of scripts that humanity has ever invented. Among living, extant scripts—apart from the Chinese script family with its six-thousand-year roots, in whose foundation no perceptible change is observed—all branch from the Phoenician script. The paintings before you are the result of the reciprocal influence of Nasta'liq calligraphy and Chinese calligraphy; both are distant offspring of prehistoric painting. The letters of Nasta'liq have taken the place of Chinese syllables, and the syllables of Chinese calligraphy have risen to the elegance and grace of Nasta'liq.

en.title: Traces of Time in Persian Calligraphy
en.description_markdown:
The Persians replaced cuneiform script with the Arabic script. This alphabet, which had fewer than 30 letters, was essentially constructed of similar straight strokes meeting at 90-degree angles. Over 15 centuries, the Persians introduced two fundamental transformations to it: the thickness of the strokes changed and the angles became varied; then, by harmonising them, curves took the place of straight strokes and angles. Through centuries of patience and love, Iran's masters of calligraphy strove to bring this calligraphy into harmony with the entirety of Persian culture.
Contemporary Iranian artists, by inventing a form of "calligraphy-painting", have enabled us to sense the beauty and delicacy of this script. Letting oneself go into the effects of the letters, forgetting time, swimming in these signs, being touched by a rain of letters, entrusting sentences and verses to the play of time—this is what I wish to place before your eyes.
Where are the letters that, a thousand years ago, flowed from the hands of masters onto handwritten books? Where are the words that the Mongols burnt? Where are the poems lost in the deserts, dissolved into the imaginings and dreams of a nation? Where are the curves thanks to which a people beheld the mirror of the universe? I seek them...

en.title: How Green I Am Today
en.description_markdown:
[This series of paintings came to life through my hand and pen, inspired by the poem of the late Sohrab Sepehri.](/fa/media/videos/ghalimanchehsabzmamroz-fa)

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/Tableau-2-1.jpg

Based on this poem by [Sohrab Sepehri](http://www.teheran.ir/spip.php?article1196), *How Green I Am Today*, before you is a series of paintings.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/Tableau-2-1.jpg

[A film on the carpet painting titled "How Green I Am Today"](/fr/media/videos/tapie-je-suis-si-vert-aujour-fa)

At Golestâneh

How green I am today

What vast plains
What lofty mountains
In Golestâneh, what a scent of grass filled the air!
In this village I was searching for something
For a dream, perhaps
For a light, a pebble, a smile
Behind the poplars
Lay a pure obliviousness that called out to me
I paused beside a reed-bed; the wind was blowing, I listened
Who was speaking to me?
A lizard glided past
I set out
An alfalfa field along the path
Then a cucumber patch, colourful safflower shrubs
And the oblivion of the earth
At the water's edge
I took off my cloth slippers and sat down, feet in the water

How green I am today
And how alert my body is
May no sorrow arrive from beyond the mountain

Who is behind the trees?
No one; a cow is grazing in the meadow plot
It is summer noon
The shadows know what kind of summer it is
Spotless shadows
A bright and pure corner
Children of feeling! Here is the place to play

Life is not empty
There is kindness, there are apples, there is faith
Yes, as long as there are poppies, one must live

In my heart there is something like a grove of light, like a dream at daybreak
And I am so restless that my heart longs
To run to the end of the plain, to go up to the mountaintop
In the distance, there is a voice calling me

fr.title: Je ne suis pas moi
fr.description_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg

Le texte précis et fécond de M. Farhad Zamani au sujet de cette œuvre est très instructif. Avec beaucoup de générosité, il m’a également demandé mon avis. Ces quelques lignes répondent à cette demande.

Tout d’abord, son texte :

Farhad Zamani

Cher Maître,

Il y a des années, alors que j’apprenais le nasta‘lîq, j’étais émerveillé de constater que toute la beauté de l’écriture et toute son emprise viennent de la part qui demeure invisible, qui n’est pas écrite, qui reste blanche. Par exemple, en traçant en nasta‘lîq la ligature « tam » (تم), on peut observer avec attention, au bord de la jonction, la tête d’une colombe dans la blancheur : le « tam » écrit est tangible et sensible, tandis que la tête de la colombe est impalpable.

Plus tard, j’ai lu l’exemple du potier chez Heidegger, selon lequel ce qui donne forme à la cruche et constitue la finalité de sa fabrication est son vide et son espace creux, ainsi que ce que dit Lacan, à savoir que l’art consiste à donner forme au vide, et…

J’ai vu maintes œuvres de calligraphie-peinture dont les lettres ou les expressions n’ont pas de valeur pour le propriétaire du tableau, mais où quelque chose d’indicible, de non écrit — que l’artiste lui-même ignore peut-être — suscite un attachement tel qu’il le maintient sans cesse sous son regard. Les tracés écrits, tels la paroi et le fond de la cruche, ont donné forme à l’espace vide, ont façonné les non-écrits et leur ont conféré une ouverture : une forme inachevée qui, autant qu’on la répète, se transforme sans jamais parvenir à son terme. J’ai vu plusieurs de vos tableaux et, même dans ce peu d’œuvres, l’expression « moi » (*man*) revient à maintes reprises sur les toiles ; c’est du tableau *Je ne suis pas moi* que j’ai reçu la plus vive impression. Dans la composition de l’œuvre, on peut lire le corps et distinguer trois formes écrites du « moi », chacune pouvant porter un signifié différent, etc. ; ainsi que la belle couleur jaune du fond, aurore de la conscience, et la couleur noire de l’écriture qui, dans l’émergence même de la conscience, peut former un voile sombre jusqu’à l’effacement, tel le dégradé du foncé au clair des lignes sur la conscience.

Autrement dit, un lieu où le moi conscient, imaginaire et symbolique ferait défaut — et, chose poignante, le « moi » s’efface à tel point dans la couleur jaune du fond qu’il ne laisse à l’être humain aucun outil d’expression.

Je serais heureux de connaître votre avis.

Ma réponse :

L’art donne à voir notre « vide », afin qu’autour d’un tel trou nous cultivions une vérité, afin que nous découvrions un secret nouveau de la « réalité impossible ». La vérité est singulière. La réalité est de l’ordre de l’être. Là où l’art noue une relation avec notre « vide disponible », le miracle se produit. Un voile s’écarte. Le voile est individuel. Le voile est individuel et instantané. Transparente évidence, ici et en cet instant, c’est une étincelle capable d’engendrer le feu.

La production de l’art, au sens ci-dessus, consiste à retourner le regard de l’artiste vers ce trou intérieur qui est le sien, sans l’intervention d’une volonté de transmettre une vérité préexistante en l’artiste. C’est ici que les trous peuvent échanger ensemble une parole sur la réalité. Ce dialogue, tel un réseau infini de trous et d’émerveillements, façonne un monde nouveau et éphémère.

De quelque côté que je sois allé, rien n’a fait qu’accroître mon effroi ;

Garde à ce désert et à ce chemin sans fin.

Les habitants de ce monde se trouvent et se reconnaissent les uns les autres.

Nous sommes les intimes de la retraite de l’amitié, ne t’afflige point ;

À l’ami familier, tiens un propos familier.

Ils entendent la parole familière de celui qui leur est familier.

J’ai tracé ces lettres de sorte que l’étranger n’en comprît rien ;

Toi aussi, par générosité, lis-les ainsi que toi seul sais lire.

Soyez élevé et honoré.

Hassan Makaremi

Farhad Zamani

Cher Maître,

L’attention que vous accordez à un interlocuteur aussi profane que moi, compte tenu du prix de votre temps, dépasse tout ce que je pouvais imaginer ; je vous en remercie.

Mais, sachant combien vous êtes épris de Hâfez et ayant également lu votre livre, il m’aurait été pénible de ne pas vous dire que votre expression « vide disponible » (*khâli-ye âmâdeh*) évoque la formule de Hâfez « à rebours de l’accoutumance » (*khelâf-âmad*).

Si notre vide, notre manque, constitue en termes freudiens une chose impossible, inacceptable et contraire aux usages, aux coutumes et au tabou, alors nous entendons l’accomplissement artistique dans la parole profonde de Hâfez au distique ci-dessous — contraire à l’habitude et à un caractère semblable au vide, et dénué d’habitude et de caractère :

Cherche ton vœu à l’encontre du cours de l’habitude, car moi,

C’est de cette chevelure éparse que j’ai conquis le recueillement.

en.title: I Am Not I
en.description_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg

The precise and richly insightful essay by Mr Farhad Zamani regarding this work is deeply instructive. He has also generously asked for my view. These few lines are written in response to his request.

First, his text:

Farhad Zamani

Dear Master,

Years ago, while studying Nastaliq calligraphy, I used to marvel at how the entire beauty and impact of the script stem from the part that is unseen, unwritten, left white. For example, when writing the Nastaliq ligature *tam* (تم), one can discern with careful attention the head of a dove in the white negative space along the edge of the joint: the written *tam* is tangible and perceptible, whereas the dove's head remains intangible.

Later, I read Heidegger's example of the potter, explaining that what shapes the jug and constitutes the very purpose of its making is its void and empty space, as well as Lacan's statement that art is the shaping of the void, and so forth...

I have seen many works of calligraphic painting (*naqqashi-khat*) whose letters or phrases hold no intrinsic value for the owner of the painting, yet something ineffable and unwritten—perhaps unknown even to the artist—creates such an attachment that the viewer keeps it continually before their eyes. Like the walls and base of the jug, the written strokes have given shape to the empty space, shaped what remains unwritten, and granted it an opening: an unfinished form that alters with every repetition, yet never reaches completion. I have seen several of your paintings, and even in those few works the word "I" (*man*) is repeated many times across the canvases. The deepest impression I received was from the painting *I Am Not I*: within the painting's composition, one can read the body and see three written forms of "I", each capable of carrying a different signified, and so forth—along with the beautiful yellow colour of the background, like the dawn of consciousness, and the black colour of the calligraphy, which, even as consciousness emerges, can become a dark veil tending towards effacement, like the dark-and-light tonal modulation of lines across consciousness.

In other words, a place where the conscious, Imaginary, and Symbolic "I" is absent—and, regrettably, where the "I" dissolves so completely into the yellow ground that it leaves the human being no instrument for expression.

I would be delighted to know your thoughts.

My response:

Art reveals our "emptiness", so that around such a void we may nurture a truth, so that we may uncover a new secret of "impossible reality". Truth is individual. Reality belongs to the order of being. Where art establishes a relation with our "prepared emptiness", a miracle takes place. A veil is drawn aside. The veil is individual. The veil is individual and momentary. A lucid transparency, here and in this very instant, is a spark that can kindle a fire.

The production of art, in the sense above, is the turning back of the artist's gaze towards that inner void of their own, without the intervention of any will to transmit a truth already residing within the artist. It is here that these voids can speak to one another of reality. This dialogue, like an endless network of voids and wonders, creates a new and transient world.

Whichever way I turned, nothing grew within me save dread;

Beware of this wilderness and this endless road.

The inhabitants of this world find and recognise one another.

We are the confidants of the sanctuary of intimacy—grieve not;

Speak familiar words to a familiar friend.

They hear familiar speech from one who is familiar.

I have written these letters in such a way that strangers could not understand;

You too, by the grace of your nobility, read them as only you know how.

May you stand proud and honoured.

Hassan Makaremi

Farhad Zamani

Dear Master,

Your gracious attention to a reader as uninitiated as myself, given how precious your time is, goes beyond anything I could have imagined; I thank you.

Yet, knowing how devoted an admirer of Hafez you are and having also read your book, I could not refrain from saying that your phrase "prepared emptiness" (*khali-ye amadeh*) evokes Hafez's expression "contrary to custom" (*khelaf-amad*).

If our emptiness, our void, is in Freudian terms something impossible, unacceptable, and contrary to habit, convention, and taboo, then we hear artistic fulfilment in Hafez's profound couplet below—contrary to custom and to a trait resembling a void, and emptied of habit and convention:

Seek fulfilment contrary to the course of custom, for I

Gathered inward composure from those dishevelled tresses.

en.title: Employing Nastaliq Symbols in a New Composition
en.description_markdown:
Before you lies an example of the fruit of twenty years of my work, blending a calligraphic ground with the deployment of Nastaliq symbols in a new composition: calligraphy standing somewhere between things and words, at the summit of the stylisation of symbols.

The quest for knowledge is the foundational and continuous stratum of our presence. In tracing our journey of hundreds of thousands of years between two worlds—which, for convenience, we call the animal world and the human world—many obscure regions still remain. In very brief terms, the presence of this difference may be understood as symbolisation. Symbolisation gave us the opportunity to name, and naming led us to communicate with one another and to invent "things", which come into being through being named.
Prehistoric cave art, the founding mother of writing, is the earliest surviving trace of time in human life. From prehistoric art to writing, "naming" gradually opens up its space.

And the boundaries of our presence in existence are inscribed with lines and curves, small and large, upon clay or paper, and ultimately with the modern tools of computers—as though the symbols we use in everyday life, these million-year-old vestiges, carry our past tangibly within themselves. Calligraphy creates harmony, stylises, and brings before our eyes the lines between ourselves and existence. Put another way, the calligrapher's hand stylises and brings alive before our eyes the living continuity of the beauty of forms and the acoustic image of spoken words that have been turning among us for thousands of years.

The calligrapher stands as a mediator between the image of "things" and our pre-existing sensibility for perceiving the world and the harmony of the universe that humanity has discovered.

en.title: Journey (Arrival)
en.description_markdown:
From bacteria to *Homo sapiens* spans more than three billion years, and forty thousand years separate that advent from our own time. Life continues, and the more the years accumulate, the stronger grows the resistance against death of "this thing" which, for the sake of simplicity, we call "life". It is as though the aim of life were "life" against "death". This immense journey of attaining "jouissance", passing through a crucial stage that I call the stage of "human rights", cannot stop before reaching the right to life as the sole foundational right of our "Earth". Beyond the fossils of our ancestors and the historical and architectural testimonies that remain to us as witnesses of this path, there is prehistoric rock art, there are writings, there is oral culture, there is human cultural heritage, and there are all the living species of our Earth—together with their legacy as a witness to the past and a point of departure towards the future. Until the day when something was written upon a support: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the human being stands forth as the noblest witness to these three billion years. This Journey still has fine days ahead of it: indeed, writing the right to life is establishing it and ensuring it is respected.

Perhaps—perhaps this right will lead us beyond this Earth! And perhaps this right will demand another space from us! To continue bequeathing the heritage of "life" to our children, it falls to each of us to trace this shared journey of life, each with their own means and their own medium...

Before you are the series of works *Sign to Symbol* and *Invisible Lines in Boundless Colour*. It is my journey on three levels—universal, individual, and artistic—that I share with you. And I share with you these calligraphies: the harmonious trace of the writings of this journey left by our ancestors. These invisible lines are the traces of our dreams in the Real, the silences of blues. And now it is for you to answer me. Little time remains to us. If you too would tell me of your journey... whenever you wish...

"Silence is blue to the height of the sky's eyes. Time flows to the limit of our weariness." Hassan Makaremi, 2006

The sky sees us just as we see it. Yes, it has eyes. Yes, between us and the sun lies this astonished grandeur of silence, and there is no time left for counting. Therefore, another instrument besides accounting is required.

en.title: Prehistoric Rock Art and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
en.description_markdown:
By voluntarily tracing with their hand the first line upon the wall of a cave, humankind took a step forward: they declared their distinction from the animal world, stood taller still, looked farther ahead, and said, "I can, and I know." They liberated themselves and carried their symbolism forward; this singular relationship with the self and the world had an anti-death effect for them: life became less mortal, the line endured, and it carried the inscribed message across time, for future generations.

This human being playing a wind instrument, with the traces of its music shown like dots beneath the instrument; that square upon the chief's arm—which has survived even to the present day as an insignia of rank; the rituals of sun worship, which express their faith and manifest the right to hold faith; family life, a village, and social life; the right to pleasure, through the depiction of the naked body; the right to travel, through recounting its story; by honouring scenes of production and, finally, giving form—ever more fully they express their world through symbols; the right is more psychic than social...

From bacteria to *Homo sapiens* spans more than three billion years, and forty thousand years separate that advent from our own time. Life continues, and the more the years accumulate, the stronger grows the resistance against death of "this thing" which, for the sake of simplicity, we call "life". It is as though the aim of life were "life" against "death". This immense journey of attaining "jouissance", passing through an important stage that I call the stage of "human rights", cannot stop before reaching the right to life as our sole foundational right, "the Earth". Beyond the fossils of our ancestors and the historical and architectural testimonies that remain to us as witnesses of this path, there is prehistoric rock art, there are writings, there is oral culture, there is human cultural heritage, and there are all the living specimens of our Earth. This path still has fine days ahead of it: indeed, writing the right to life is establishing it.

Perhaps—perhaps this right will guide us beyond this Earth! And perhaps this right will demand another space from us! To continue bequeathing the heritage of "life" to our children, each of us must trace this shared journey of life, each according to their own possibility... "Silence is blue to the height of the sky's eyes. Time flows to the limit of our weariness."

The sky sees us just as we see it. Yes, it has eyes. Yes, between us and the sun lies this astonished grandeur of silence, and there is no opportunity for counting. Thus, another instrument besides accounting is required.

---

His works sweep us into his imaginary world, where his humanist ideas and his gaze upon life are depicted through a blend of colours. His architectural compositions carry us into a realm where the magic of the moment expands. His calligraphies, akin to the dance of sirens, symbolise a harmony between the suppleness of a hand gliding across centuries of history and the mysterious labyrinth of Persian poetry. His colourist compositions open our gaze at times upon an impressionist world, and at times upon the delicacy of Persian miniature painting.

Concerning his work *Prehistoric Rock Art and Human Rights* (fresco, 6 square metres), he tells us:
"From the caves towards the moon. From the earliest traces of symbolisation—cave paintings—to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: this distance of some forty thousand years, of efforts to expand the fields of our knowledge and our well-being, is a long crossing. The prehistoric drawings discovered to date across the five continents, with the diversity of their symbolisations and the means employed, speak of hope, of the journey, of the aspiration for peace, of family life, of discoveries, of astonishment before the universe, and finally of relations with the Other and with nature."

Following his encounter with psychoanalysis, the painter developed another perspective on the Persian cultural movement stretching from 7000 BCE to the present day. Since the representation of bodies was forbidden in Islam, art and literature manifested themselves around Architecture, Poetry, and Calligraphy. He clarifies his thought on this subject:
"Naturally, this three-dimensional knot—Architecture, Poetry, and Calligraphy—carries within itself the three modes of human knowledge:

- the effect of reality (geography, ways of life, climate, nature, plants, flowers, and desert),
- the effect of the Imaginary, of dreams, fantasies, hopes, desires,
- and finally the effects of the Symbolic, embodied in culture, in gestures, in signifiers, words, ways of moving, movements of the body, ways of turning the eyes, dances...

What is repressed returns; the deep layers of mythologies, architectural elements, rituals, and foundational principles manifest themselves.
What I seek, through this sensibility, is the illustration of the coherence and harmony of this image of 'a parallel world', through calligraphy, painting, the image of architecture within painting, the image of drawings and curves within calligraphy, the curves of domes within alphabets—and perhaps, in the future, the deepest traces of symbolisations: traces of rock art within these signs and symbols."

en.title: The Conference of the Birds (Simorq)
en.description_markdown:
This painting, measuring 210 by 1,000 centimetres, was created in Paris in 2006 and 2007 after the epic poem *The Conference of the Birds* (*Manteq al-Tayr*) by the venerable Farîd al-Dîn Attâr of Nishapur. It begins on the right with "The birds of the world held an assembly"—an image of the globe and the birds gathered upon it—and points to the seven stages and valleys through which these birds were destined to pass. And at the end, with the rising of the sun, thirty birds (*si morgh*) reach Mount Qaf, whose reflection is the Simorq itself. At this stage, on the right side, sits a convex mirror in which all the birds—just as Attâr relates—behold themselves and all that has passed, and so too does the viewer.

[A short film introducing this painting](/fa/media/videos/simorq-tablo-ir)

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· First Valley: The Valley of Quest (*Talab*): Awakening; a living being enters life, takes its destiny into its own hands, and presses forward amid critical and arduous conditions: from Christopher Columbus to Yuri Gagarin, towards the sky, upon the moon, or in thought and imagination, in search of the essence of life which, like the alchemists, one may call the "subtle essence" (*latifeh*).

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· Second Valley: The Valley of Love (*'Eshq*): The agent of movement and force, with diverse definitions of love: Sigmund Freud regards its foundational model as the relationship between mother and child—a state of unity born of separation and connection, a state that grants us the capacity to perceive the "Other", an Other that may be indefinable, all too close, something that after awakening does not let us fall back asleep: birth and newness.

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· Third Valley: The Valley of Knowledge (*Ma'refat*): Knowledge of one's own presence after birth; this presence enables each of us to recognise the Other through observation, comparison, and the emergence of the symbol from prehistoric art to its place today...

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· Fourth Valley: The Valley of Independence (*Esteqlal*): If I am one element among other elements, I hold an equal value and can receive nothing beyond what is due to me. Let us listen to Hafez, celebrant of love, a bird from another world:

Such a cage is unworthy of a sweet singer like me;

I shall fly to the garden of Paradise, for I am a bird of that meadow.

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· Fifth Valley: The Valley of Unity (*Yeganegi*): Following such knowledge and such unity, the first sense of arrival, companionship, and reasoning; in this domain of Iranian mysticism, "Hu" means "He" or, more simply, "the Other"—only "the Other" exists.

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· Sixth Valley: The Valley of Bewilderment (*Heyrat*): Bewilderment before the depth of my place; my eyes open wide and I see far into the distance, forever and irrevocably.

The experience of the mystical journey, an example of observing life through the mystical school of the tenth to fourteenth centuries CE: the Seven Valleys:

· Seventh Valley: Poverty and Annihilation (*Faqr o Fana*): Life, in its simplicity, just as Hafez shows it:

Dust-laden with poverty as I am, shame upon my high resolve

Were I to moisten my hem in the waters of the sun's own spring.

---

## Painting — 2 m × 10 m — "The Conference of the Birds"

The centrepiece of the exhibition, this work pairs an initiation into tradition with a contemporary practice of *Pardeh Dari*. In a modern idiom, the painting recounts the essence of the tale of *The Conference of the Birds*, grounded in the myth of the Simorq. In Persian mythology, the figure of the Simorq, dwelling upon the mythical Mount Qaf, holds supreme significance. This 20-square-metre canvas was produced between 2005 and 2007. In this painting, I illustrate the story of *The Conference of the Birds* by Farîd al-Dîn Attâr, the Persian poet who lived from 1119 to 1190 and belongs to the great Iranian mystical tradition (*Le Langage des oiseaux*, paperback edition, by Farîd al-Dîn Attâr, translated by Garcin de Tassy).

*The Conference of the Birds* comprises 4,647 verses. It is a mystical epic in which birds set off in search of their King. The narrative opens with a welcoming discourse serving a ritual and magical function that binds the "Hoopoe"—a crested bird wearing a crown—to the other birds, who represent a seeking humanity. Immediately, the throng of anxious birds gathers, and providentially the Hoopoe steps forward as messenger. It exhorts the birds to embark on a perilous journey that will lead them to the court of their King, a fabulous bird, the Simorq. All the birds grasp the fundamental importance of this undertaking; yet almost at once, the majority make excuses. The Hoopoe admonishes them all, reassures some, encourages others, and begins the instruction that will enable them to set out on the voyage. They must enter the seven valleys that mark the initiatory stages of their spiritual ascent. These mystical valleys are the valleys of quest, love, knowledge, independence, union, bewilderment, and destitution. Only after traversing these valleys over a long journey in which the vast majority of the birds perish do the survivors find themselves—as a final ordeal—refused entry to the long-hoped-for palace of their King: the Simorq. The form chosen is the modern manifestation of *Pardeh Dari*, a pre-Islamic Iranian storytelling art that has undergone two transformations since its origins. Drawing on the narrative of *The Conference of the Birds*, the painting goes in search of a place other than this real world already encountered and another imaginary world.

en.title: Are Our Worlds Not a Torus?
en.description_markdown:
#### https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/2012-05-05-20.44.30-Copier.jpg

#### "Man nah manam, nah man manam" ("I am not I, nor am I myself")—this is the opening hemistich of the beautiful ghazal by Asiri Lahiji, which can evoke the discourse of the torus in the Lacanian topology of our psyche. In these three words, the poet brings forward humanity's most fundamental question: the boundaries between the "I" and the Other, or the presence of the "I" within the being of the Other. Such an indivisible, unbreakable "I", through the extraordinary presence of symbolisation and by gaining access to the dimension of communication made possible through these very symbols, enters into relation with the Other as well as with the past, present, and future; the "I" emerges from stasis and creates another "I". Human presence in the world, given the knowledge attained thus far, may be recalled across four worlds: the tangible and observable world, the measurable world, the possible world, and the world that holds the Subject within its grasp. Working upon this profound poem and its relationship with the Lacanian torus and the imaginal world has guided me towards the paintings below.

In his method of introducing his distinctive topology, Jacques Lacan likens the human individual to a torus—a torus being a three-dimensional figure generated by rotating a circle in three-dimensional space around an axis that is coplanar with, yet non-tangent to, that circle—such that the individual's body resembles the surface of the torus, the interior of the torus constitutes the individual's psyche, and the exterior of the torus constitutes the individual's external world (Figure 1). By piercing a hole in the body of this torus, one can reach a hand inside and turn the torus inside out. Through this operation, we observe that what is on the outside passes to the inside and what is on the inside passes to the outside.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/Sans-titre.png

The role of parallel time: In this regard, the foundational concepts are as follows: the celestial "I", the spiritual earth (*zamin-e minovi*), the eighth space, parallel time, and three modes of human perception: perception through the senses; perception through concepts; and etheric or *Hurqalya* perception, or the imaginal world (*mundus imaginalis*). Henry Corbin grasped these concepts with remarkable precision and explains them thus: encountering the Earth not merely as a collection of material factors, but in the person of its angel, is a psychic event that manifests neither in the realm of impersonal abstract concepts nor in sensory data. The Earth must be perceived not solely through the senses, but through a primordial image, for this image possesses its own singular quality. In other words, this image is a reflection of the very self that the psyche alone bears within itself. Orientation in time: the various ways in which human beings substantiate their presence upon Earth, and the continuity of this presence in something like history, raise the question of whether this continuity itself possesses a distinct meaning. For the pinnacle of Iranian mysticism is attaining the Orient—an Orient that can be known through an integral perception, which is neither localisable nor contained upon a geographical map; an Orient situated in none of the seven climes, continents, or regions. In truth, it is an eighth continent. Such a mystical Orient, beyond sensory perceptions, the place of departure and return, the object of perpetual quest, is the celestial pole itself.
Orientation is one of the primal phenomena of our presence in the world. Being human is, in its essence, conferring space upon the world around oneself—a phenomenon that gives rise to the human being's relationship with their surroundings. The four cardinal points—east, west, south, and north—are not things encountered by human presence, but rather directions with which human experience and concrete presence are familiar. Possessing this sense makes orientation in the world possible. Imaginary lines, east to west or north to south, weave a network of manifest imaginary lines without which neither geographical orientation nor human orientation is possible. Whatever name we give them, the events that define the relationship with each person's unseen guide cannot be situated within countable material time. They cannot be measured by continuous, uniform, homogeneous units of time regulated by the motions of celestial bodies. This is a psychic and discontinuous time, of pure quality, whose moments cannot be assessed except by measuring them against themselves—a unit of measurement that alters each time according to their density, in such a way that the past is present in the future and the future in the past. Like the notes of a musical phrase, they arrive one after another yet are all present together in order to constitute the musical phrase.
Indeed, the accounts above may be summarised as follows: according to Iranian beliefs, our life in this time and upon this Earth is accompanied by another life—the life of our psyche, which dwells in parallel in another world (the spiritual earth, *zamin-e minovi*). The presence of such a parallel time and our relationship with it in the life of pre-Islamic Iranians were transmitted through diverse schools of Illuminationist mysticism (*'erfan-e eshraqi*) into Shi'ism and found their place within Shi'i traditions.

---

"Man nah manam, nah man manam" — "I am not I, not I, I am" — "What if our universe were a torus!" Through this verse, the poet proclaims a state of human being that profoundly questions its own boundaries: a presence of the ego (*moi*) in another Universe. This indivisible individual—who through the magic of symbolisation, through integrating the dimensions of communication made possible by symbols, and through the fluidity with which symbols circulate between self and others, between past, present, and future, shatters the immobile status of the individual and invents another ego, an ego swimming in symbols, unbound by time or space. The presence of a human Subject in their Universe concentrates within them their entire culture; from there the Subject sets forth their discourse. "I am not I...": this poetic utterance is an introductory step in the negation of the Subject and therefore merits deep inquiry. The Universe is individual, even though our knowledge and scholarship to date guide us to classify at least four families of the Universe: the visible Universe, the measurable Universe, the possible Universe, and the Universe encompassing the presence of a Subject. The earliest apes enable us to imagine the Universe of the speaking being thanks to traces of gestural symbolisations. Then come intermediate objects, rituals, syllables, words, spoken utterances, prehistoric drawings, and the earliest elements of writing. The tales of shamans, mythologies, and oral culture present another facet of this Universe. Dream, fantasy, poetry, and art constitute further dimensions of it. Henry Corbin, the great twentieth-century French scholar, in dissecting pre-Islamic Persian culture and mythology and their continuity within the thought of Iranian mystics, reveals to us the presence of a parallel world—neither this world nor the other world after death: a clime, a continent present yet inaccessible to us save for rare exceptions. A part of our presence as a human Subject dwells within that world. It is *Ravan*, a concept untranslatable by our notion of *psyche*. As though this world—the third—were neither this present internal world nor our absent external world of the imaginable Universe, but genuinely between the two. Jacques Lacan, the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, speaks of a Universe of signifiers circulating among "speaking beings" (*êtres parlants*) that belongs to no one—neither internal nor external, situated in a third place. What if our Universe were a Torus! There is an exterior within the interior, or an interior outside. A torus is generated by the rotation of a circle around another circle. What if, after all, this exterior–interior or interior–exterior divided our Universe differently? Calling the boundaries of the ego into question is, perhaps, not unrelated to this sense of presence. Beyond symbolisation, there also lie traces of self-construction—frontiers difficult to explore with the tools of symbolisation alone. If writing is the summit of our ancestors' collective symbolisation, enabling entry into the world of science, and if art, music, dance, and the plastic arts are noble vehicles for manifesting knowledge and our intuitions, may we not say that calligraphy is the stylisation of this symbolisation, employing the harmony created by art? What stands before you is an endeavour to bring a story back to life. *The Torus Universe*, represented through elements of the Persian world's environment alongside Nastaliq or Parsi calligraphy and their intimate relationship, embodies the harmony of this atmosphere.

Hassan Makaremi, Paris, 2011
